At birth, the wet weight of a fawn averages around 3600 grams [Wwb = around 3600 grams], a value that varies latitudinally with maternal body condition and local forage quality. This initial mass is modest relative to the species' ultimate size but provides sufficient reserves for thermoregulation during the first days of life. Newborn fawns are precocial, capable of standing and following the dam within hours of parturition, a behavioral adaptation that reduces predation risk during the vulnerable neonatal period. The rapid skeletal elongation observed in the first weeks of life, measured as increases in total body length, reflects the intense selective pressure for fawns to outgrow the gape size of medium-sized canid predators.

This fecundity is among the highest recorded for North American cervids of comparable body size and is facilitated by a relatively short gestation period. Females in prime condition on high-quality ranges are the most likely to produce triplets, whereas yearling or nutritionally stressed does more commonly bear singletons. The annual reproductive schedule is synchronized with the spring flush of vegetative growth, ensuring that peak lactation coincides with maximal forage quality and availability. This temporal alignment represents a critical life-history adaptation to seasonal environments where resource abundance is concentrated into a brief growing season.

Embryonic development includes a period of obligate diapause, or delayed implantation, during which the blastocyst remains quiescent in the uterine lumen for several weeks before attaching to the endometrium. This reproductive strategy allows females to mate in the autumn, when body condition is at its seasonal peak following summer foraging, while still scheduling birth for the following spring when neonatal survival prospects are highest. Male fawns typically achieve puberty slightly later than females, a pattern common among polygynous cervids where body size confers a competitive advantage during the rut.
